stories.title: Forget Property Deeds: The Moon’s Real Estate Could Run on Operating Rights

Barriers to entry are eroding. The promise of resources is growing. And as scientific missions justify infrastructure, this could support commercial activity, which in turn will generate assets. Some of that activity could stray into the realm of commercial real estate. But don’t expect lunar deeds and property lines to look much like their terrestrial counterparts. “The lunar economy is still in its early stages,” Raquel Buscaino, Head of Novel & Exponential Technologies (NExT), Deloitte Consulting LLP, told Connect CRE. “Once a foundational infrastructure is established, it could support downstream activity in areas including resources and materials, space data, manufacturing, and other services.” Where the Necessities Are Transportation and logistics, power, communications and navigation, construction, and life-support systems will need to come first before a broader commercial ecosystem can develop. One challenge is that the resources needed to sustain a long-term presence are located in one of the Moon’s most difficult environments: the lunar South Pole. On the plus side, some South Pole locations receive near-continuous sunlight for solar power and are close to permanently shadowed craters that could contain water ice. bullets: Deloitte report signals lunar economy moving from niche to fast-moving frontier.
Commercial real estate activity on moon unlikely within multifamily development timelines.
Infrastructure (transportation, power, comms, life-support) must precede commercial ecosystem development.
stories.summary: Deloitte's 'Building the Lunar Economy' report describes the lunar economy as rapidly eroding barriers to entry and building momentum. Transportation, logistics, power, communications, and life-support systems must be established before broader commercial activity can develop. While some activity could eventually touch commercial real estate, this remains exploratory and decades away.
stories.impact: No material impact to multifamily development. Lunar economy remains speculative and far outside relevant capital deployment and demand cycles for apartment communities.

stories.title: Fifth Third Bank Expands Offices at 50 Rockefeller Plaza
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer announced that Fifth Third Bank has expanded its offices at 50 Rockefeller Plaza at Rockefeller Center, increasing its footprint at the building to 32,347 square feet. Fifth Third Bank first leased space at Rockefeller Center in October 2022 and has now expanded by nearly 11,000 square feet. The expansion is coterminous with the bank’s existing lease through February 2034. “Fifth Third Bank’s expansion is a strong endorsement of the workplace experience we continue to build across the Rockefeller Center campus,” said EB Kelly, Senior Managing Director at Tishman Speyer and Head of Rockefeller Center. “Since joining the campus in 2022, Fifth Third has become a valued part of our community, and we’re pleased to support their continued growth in New York.” In the lease transaction, Fifth Third Bank was represented by Joe Cabrera, Kevin Torch and Michael Ciotta. Tishman Speyer was represented in-house by Blythe Kinsler. The post Fifth Third Bank Expands Offices at 50 Rockefeller Plaza appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Fifth Third Bank expands Manhattan office by 11,000 sf at 50 Rockefeller Plaza.
Lease extended through February 2034, signaling confidence in NYC office market.
Bank's growth since October 2022 entry shows Manhattan as strategic location.
stories.summary: Fifth Third Bank expanded its footprint at Rockefeller Center by nearly 11,000 square feet to 32,347 total sf, with the lease coterminous through February 2034. The bank first entered the campus in October 2022 and has now grown its presence, indicating commitment to its Manhattan operations. Tishman Speyer highlighted the expansion as an endorsement of the workplace experience at Rockefeller Center.
stories.impact: Modest positive signal for NYC office occupancy stability, but limited direct bearing on multifamily. Bank expansion in Manhattan signals continued corporate investment and executive/employee presence, which sustains underlying rental demand in nearby residential submarkets like Midtown East and Plaza District, though this effect is already baked into current market pricing.

stories.title: Colliers Markets Senior Loan on DTLA’s EY Plaza
stories.excerpt: Colliers has launched the marketing of the senior loan secured by EY Plaza, the 41-story, 968,745-square-foot office tower at 725 S. Figueroa St. in Downtown Los Angeles, on behalf of the lender. The loan is held in a single-asset, single-borrower securitization, and the property is operated under a court-appointed receiver. Offers are due in October. The offering comes as Downtown Los Angeles office acquisition activity increasingly favors owner-users. Recent purchases by organizations, including Capital Group, Los Angeles County, Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, Southwest Carpenters Pension Trust, and L.A. Care Health Plan, have shifted nearly five million square feet of inventory toward occupant ownership. “Buyers aren’t pricing Downtown Los Angeles as a submarket anymore. They’re underwriting each tower on its own floorplates, tenancy and owner-user potential,” said Sean Fulp, Vice Chair at Colliers. “That’s why two buildings a few blocks apart can trade at very different values.” Alongside Fulp, the Colliers investment sales team includes Executive Vice Presidents Todd Tydlaska and Mark Schuessler and Associate Vice Presidents Jordan Garcia and Blake Hammerstein. The leasing team includes Vice Chair Matt Heyn, Executive Vice President Ian Gilbert, and Senior Vice President Kurt Davis. The post Colliers Markets Senior Loan on DTLA’s EY Plaza appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: EY Plaza (968k sf, 41-story tower) senior loan marketed in DTLA distress.
Property operates under court-appointed receiver; offers due October.
DTLA office market increasingly favors owner-user purchases over investor acquisitions.
stories.summary: Colliers is marketing a senior loan secured by EY Plaza, a 968,745-square-foot office tower at 725 S. Figueroa in Downtown Los Angeles, on behalf of the lender. The property is held in a single-asset securitization and is under court-appointed receivership. Offers are due in October. Recent market activity shows DTLA office increasingly dominated by owner-user purchases (Capital Group, LA County, LA DWP, etc.), with nearly five million square feet shifting to occupant ownership.
stories.impact: DTLA office weakness signals potential long-term undersupply of downtown jobs and anchor tenants, which could depress multifamily demand in central LA submarkets (Downtown, Arts District, NoHo) over the near-to-medium term. Developer focus should pivot toward submarkets with stronger employment anchors (Playa Vista, Santa Monica, West LA tech corridors) or mixed-use sites in DTLA that capture owner-user conversions and reduce office vacancy drag.

stories.title: Beer-Importing Holterbosch Family Offloads LIC Warehouse for $95M
stories.excerpt: The Holterbosch family, former owners of a German beer importing and distribution business, has sold a Long Island City, Queens, warehouse a decade after the death of its patriarch. Dallas-based Ground Lease REIT, an affiliate of commercial real estate private equity firm Montgomery Street Partners, bought the property at 10-01 45th Road on the Long Island City waterfront for $95 million, according to a deed filing in property records made public Thursday. The Holterbosch clan has held the property since about 1968, public records indicate, despite the death of H. Dieter Holterbosch in 2016 at age 95. The company is named Hans Holterbosch Inc. and honors its founder who died in 1960. It is not clear if the company, once a major importer and distributor of Lowenbrau beer, is still active. Dieter’s daughter Heidi, who seems to have been his only survivor, signed the paperwork for the deed transfer to Ground Lease REIT. It’s unclear who brokered the deal. The Holterbosch family, which lists an office address at 375 Park Avenue, could not be reached for comment, while Ground Lease REIT did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The property along Vernon Boulevard is just feet from the Eleventh Street Basin inlet of the East River, which probably served as a logistical benefit in the past, and could also offer Ground Lease REIT development opportunities as the neighborhood continues to transform. In 2017, Heidi Holterbosch was looking for a buyer for an 8-acre site hugging Newtown Creek at 55-01 Second Street, which had been rezoned as residential as the city prepared for the redevelopment of Hunters Point South. Listed for $350 million, that site was eventually razed by TF Cornerstone to make way for housing developments in 2021. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Ground Lease REIT (Montgomery Street Partners affiliate) buys 10-01 45th Road waterfront warehouse, LIC, Queens for $95M.
Holterbosch family held property since ~1968; sale occurs decade after patriarch's 2016 death.
LIC waterfront industrial inventory turning over to institutional capital; potential rezoning/adaptive use risk.
stories.summary: The Holterbosch family sold their Long Island City waterfront warehouse at 10-01 45th Road to Ground Lease REIT (affiliate of Montgomery Street Partners) for $95 million. The family had held the industrial property since approximately 1968, when it was active in German beer importing and distribution. The sale signals a generational wealth transition and shift of LIC industrial holdings to institutional real estate ownership.
stories.impact: LIC waterfront industrial land increasingly held by institutional capital seeking ground-lease or adaptive-use conversion opportunities. Multifamily developers should monitor waterfront industrial sites (particularly along Queens Street, Jackson Avenue corridors) for rezoning or redevelopment availability; rising valuations may compress feasibility for new apartment supply in LIC's tighter footprint, supporting rents in near-market properties like Eagle Lofts.

stories.title: Juanita’s Foods to Consolidate L.A. Production at 120K-SF Facility
stories.excerpt: An 80-year-old food manufacturer is consolidating its Southern California operations into a new 120,000-square-foot facility in Santa Fe Springs, in the first deal backed by a recently formed alliance of four Los Angeles County industrial cities. Juanita’s Foods will move production from its longtime Wilmington plant to 13100 Arctic Circle in Santa Fe Springs. The deal includes an incentives agreement as well as expedited permitting via the four-city partnership. Records show LBA Logistics acquired the facility in December 2019. The cities of Commerce, Santa Fe Springs, Vernon and the City of Industry formed the Big 4 partnership in October 2025 as an economic-development coalition to coordinate investment attraction rather than compete for the same industrial employers. Together, the four cities offer about 250 million square feet of industrial space, and host more than 5,000 businesses with a workforce of about 200,000. The Big 4 cities estimate their combined industrial base generates roughly $33 billion in economic activity. “This is what becomes possible when cities stop looking at economic development as a competition and start looking at it as a regional opportunity,” Santa Fe Springs City Manager René Bobadilla said in a statement. Juanita’s said it considered locations around the country before deciding to remain in Southern California. “We conducted an exhaustive nationwide search before deciding where Juanita’s Foods would build its next chapter,” Chief Operating Officer Jody Jordan said. He cited Santa Fe Springs’ approach to business and the incentive package as key factors in the decision. LBA Logistics did not immediately return a request for comment. In May 2025, Juanita’s Foods sold a majority stake to Miami-based private equity firm Apex Capital as part of the founding De La Torre family’s estate planning. The family retained a minority interest and remains involved in operations. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.co
bullets: Juanita's Foods consolidates Southern California production into 120k sf Santa Fe Springs facility.
Big 4 cities partnership (Commerce, Santa Fe Springs, Vernon, City of Industry) formed Oct 2025 to coordinate industrial attraction.
Four-city industrial base: ~250M sf inventory, 5k+ businesses, 200k workforce, $33B annual economic activity.
stories.summary: Juanita's Foods, an 80-year-old food manufacturer, is consolidating Southern California operations into a new 120,000-square-foot facility in Santa Fe Springs via an incentives agreement and expedited permitting. The deal is the first backed by the 'Big 4' industrial partnership launched in October 2025 by Commerce, Santa Fe Springs, Vernon, and City of Industry. The four-city coalition controls ~250 million square feet of industrial inventory, hosts 5,000+ businesses, and generates approximately $33 billion in annual economic activity.
stories.impact: LA County industrial consolidation trends favor inland warehouse hubs (Santa Fe Springs, Vernon) over port-adjacent or urban-infill sites, reducing supply-chain job clusters in transit-accessible urban areas and shifting workforce commute patterns. Multifamily developers should note demand tailwinds in suburban warehouse markets (Long Beach, Inland Empire) offset by weaker downtown LA office and compressed job density in core LA neighborhoods, supporting suburban apartment rent growth over central LA.

stories.title: Knighthead Lends $63M or Doral, Fla., Industrial Portfolio Buy
stories.excerpt: Midtown Capital Partners has sealed $62.92 million of acquisition financing to fund its purchase of 13 urban-infill, small-bay industrial assets in Doral, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Knighthead Funding provided the loan for Midtown’s $86 million off-market acquisition of the 290,000-square-foot portfolio spanning 13.33 acres, according to the lender. Midtown purchased the properties from Wes Realty in August at a near-record industrial sales price for Miami-Dade County, The Real Deal previously reported. The 13 properties were developed and assembled over the last 30 years, according to Knighthead, which originated the deal with a team led by Jonathan Daniel, Alexandra Wiggins and Joseph Marraccini. “This transaction epitomizes what we look for when financing a deal — an attractive collection of assets with significant upside in an excellent infill location,” Wiggins, vice president at Knighthead Funding, said in a statement. The properties, which are located west of Miami within a mile of Miami International Airport, benefit from strong demand for small-bay industrial properties in South Florida, where vacancy rates are below 3 percent, according to Knighthead. Arrow Real Estate Advisors arranged the debt with a team consisting of Morris Betesh, Morris Dabbah and Zach Strauss. “Urban-infill portfolios like this come around once in a lifetime,” Betesh, founder and managing partner at Arrow, said in a statement. “We’ve seen the small-bay industrial sector mature significantly over the last several years, and this acquisition, along with the capital markets’ reception to the transaction, is another indication of how increasingly institutional the asset class has become.” Midtown Capital Partners did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Knighthead Funding provides $62.92M acquisition loan to Midtown Capital Partners for Doral industrial portfolio.
Midtown purchased 13 small-bay, urban-infill industrial assets (290k sf, 13.33 acres) from Wes Realty in August for $86M.
Properties located west of Miami within 1 mile of Miami International Airport at near-record industrial sales price for Miami-Dade.
stories.summary: Knighthead Funding closed $62.92 million in acquisition financing for Midtown Capital Partners' $86 million off-market purchase of a 13-asset, 290,000-square-foot industrial portfolio in Doral, Florida. The properties span 13.33 acres and were developed and assembled over 30 years. Located west of Miami within one mile of Miami International Airport, the deal represents near-record pricing for Miami-Dade County industrial assets.
stories.impact: Miami-Dade industrial market near-record valuations signal strong logistics demand driven by air-cargo, e-commerce, and Caribbean/Latin American trade flows. This capital intensity in industrial may compress multifamily development feasibility in Doral and nearby West Miami submarkets due to land scarcity and rising land costs; developers should prioritize interior Miami-Dade and Broward County suburban submarkets (Wynwood, Allapattah, Pembroke Pines) with lower industrial competition and stronger residential density zoning.

stories.title: Ares Management, PSP Investments Form $2.4B U.S. Logistics Partnership
stories.excerpt: Ares Management is diving deeper into the waters of U.S. logistics. The $670 billion private equity powerhouse announced Wednesday that it has formed a joint venture with Canada’s Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) to invest up to $2.4 billion into the development and acquisition of U.S. logistics facilities. Ares plans to combine its vertically integrated logistics real estate platform, Marq Logistics, with PSP’s scaled capital to invest into “high-conviction markets” and “strategically placed logistics facilities,” according to a release. Dave Fazekas, head of North America logistics at Ares Real Estate, noted in a statement that his firm was motivated to invest into domestic logistics hubs due to resurgent onshoring trends, growth of digital infrastructure construction, and the economy’s ongoing reliance on e-commerce. “We are proud to expand Ares’ long-standing relationship with PSP Investments as we leverage our collective scale and experience to identify compelling deployment opportunities and deliver value for tenants, communities and investors,” he said. The joint venture already plans to invest in a 5.2 million-square-foot seed portfolio of 14 assets in California, Texas and New Jersey. Laurence Bastien, managing director of real estate investments for the Americas at PSP Investments, emphasized in a statement that the U.S. logistics sector is currently defined by “durable demand drivers and structurally constrained supply,” and the partnership with Ares provides his firm with an operating platform that will “drive value at the asset level.” “Best-in-class operators, in sectors where our conviction is strongest — that is what our real estate strategy is built around, and this joint venture has both,” added Bastien. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Ares Management and PSP Investments (Canada) form $2.4B joint venture for US logistics facility development/acquisition.
Ares combining vertically integrated Marq Logistics platform with PSP's institutional capital targeting 'high-conviction markets.'
Investment thesis: onshoring, digital infrastructure growth, e-commerce reliance sustaining domestic logistics demand.
stories.summary: Ares Management announced a joint venture with Canada's Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) to deploy up to $2.4 billion into U.S. logistics real estate development and acquisition. Ares will leverage its Marq Logistics platform combined with PSP's scaled capital to target high-conviction markets and strategically placed logistics facilities. Ares cited onshoring trends, digital infrastructure construction growth, and sustained e-commerce reliance as key investment drivers.
stories.impact: Mega-cap institutional capital flooding logistics sector reinforces land and lease competition in key infill submarkets (Southern California, Texas, Northern New Jersey, Atlanta). Multifamily developers should expect industrial land scarcity and cost inflation in logistics-rich metros; consider shifting focus to secondary gateway metros and non-logistics industrial nodes, or pivot to mixed-use development capturing logistics employment clusters with above-market residential capture rates.

stories.title: Wells Fargo Refis Long Island City Apartments With $115M Fannie Mae Loan
stories.excerpt: An affiliate of Rockrose Development has secured $115 million of agency-backed debt to refinance a newly completed multifamily complex in Long Island City, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned. Wells Fargo Multifamily Capital closed the Fannie Mae-backed loan for Rockrose’s 301-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2, which opened last year in Long Island City’s Court Square neighborhood. The 19-story building on 43-14 Queens Street shares a lobby and amenities with Rockrose’s adjacent 790-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 1 tower. Avison Young negotiated the debt with a tri-state debt and equity finance team consisting of Scott Singer, Andy Singer, Kevin Swartz and Kathleen McSharry. “Long Island City remains one of the region’s most compelling multifamily markets, driven by strong residential demand, extraordinarily convenient transportation, and ongoing neighborhood growth,” Scott Singer, principal at Avison Young, said in a statement. “Phase 2 has further elevated Rockrose’s earlier Phase 1 of the Eagle Lofts Collection.” Seventy percent of apartments at Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2 are market rate with 30 percent of the units designated as affordable housing. The property’s amenities include a spa with saunas, a bowling alley, a golf simulator and a rooftop pool. Wells Fargo originated the loan with a team led by Pete Cannava, head of multifamily capital and community lending and Investment; Philip Maniscalco, head of production for multifamily capital; and Brian Antonuccio, head of East Coast production. “With 301 new residences, nearly a third of them affordable, Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2 meaningfully expands housing access in Long Island City,” Maniscalco said in a statement. Richard Brancato, chief operating officer at Rockrose, said in a statement, the transaction “reflects the strength” of its “long-standing relationships” with Wells Fargo and Avison Young. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Wells Fargo closes $115M Fannie Mae refi for Rockrose's 301-unit Eagle Lofts Phase 2, Long Island City.
Phase 2 (19-story, 301 units) shares lobby/amenities with adjacent Phase 1 (790 units); completed last year.
Agency financing at scale validates LIC Court Square as trophy multifamily market with strong rental demand.
stories.summary: Rockrose Development secured $115 million in Fannie Mae-backed agency debt through Wells Fargo to refinance its newly completed 301-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2 in Long Island City, Queens. The 19-story building at 43-14 Queens Street shares amenities and lobby with the adjacent 790-unit Phase 1 tower. Avison Young's tri-state debt team negotiated the refinance, citing strong residential demand, transportation access, and ongoing neighborhood growth.
stories.impact: Large-balance agency refi for recently-delivered LIC multifamily confirms strong investor appetite and low refinance risk in Queens luxury rental market; signals continued capital availability for stabilized LIC supply. Developers should accelerate lease-up and near-completion phase conversion to agency debt before rate/spread environment tightens; LIC's constrained waterfront land and strong transit fundamentals support continued rent growth, justifying aggressive underwriting of pre-leasing and early-stage value-add assets in Court Square and Anable Basin submarkets.
